title: a16z runs 11,307 agent shopping tests: 5 rules for when AI agents buy
summary: Next time an AI agent picks your headphones, chooses your software, or books your hotel, how do merchants get picked? a16z partnered with The Prompting Company to run 11,307 agent tests and pulled out five rules for selling to AI agents.
ai_summary: a16z and The Prompting Company ran 11,307 shopping tests across four personal agents using 1,270 prompts, plus 2,619 comparison requests on ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. The findings: agents' default recommendations overlap heavily—a product picked by one agent had a 73% chance of being picked by another; at the same price, agents chose the better return policy 86% of the time; discounts under 10% had no effect and discounts over 50% made agents steer clear. Best for brand, e-commerce, and SaaS practitioners; caveats are that the sample covers only a specific test window and four agents, the YipitData panel excludes Amazon, and a16z discloses that it and its partner may have commercial or investment interests.
brief: A product picked by one agent had a 73% chance of being picked by another; in nearly a quarter of cases, all four agents chose the same product.
At the same price, agents chose the better return policy 86% of the time; discounts under 10% didn't matter and anything over 50% made them steer clear.
Specific needs flip the default: in a broad comparison the Shark won 91% of the time; for fine or color-treated hair, Dyson won 51%; for daily use, Dyson won 88%.
On stores with guest checkout, agents made it through checkout 81% of the time; on stores requiring login, every run stalled early.

sections.h: What this is: testing AI agents as customers

blocks.p: This is the second piece on the B2A economy by a16z (Andreessen Horowitz) partners Olivia Moore and Justine Moore. B2A stands for Business-to-Agent: merchants no longer sell only to people, but also to AI agents that pick products and prepare purchases for users.

This time they worked with The Prompting Company, an agent testing firm whose customers include NVIDIA, Google, and Databricks, to run 11,307 completed agent runs across 1,270 prompts from October 22 to November 8, 2026, using four shopping agents: Grok Bot, Muse, Instinct, and Dots. They also ran 2,619 shopping requests on ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity as a comparison. The tests covered physical products and software, and sample sizes varied by experiment.

For real-world spending, they cite YipitData card-panel analysis through November 11, 2026, tracing where purchases facilitated by Muse and other consumer agents went, and they share the top 50 merchants by agent spend. Note that YipitData's tracking does not distinguish Muse from Instinct and excludes Amazon, so the rankings and dollar amounts represent only that sample, not total merchant revenue.

sections.h: Why default picks decide everything: agents converge on the same products

blocks.p: Takeaway one: for broad requests, agents often converge on a shared set of default picks. In the tests, a product picked by one agent had a 73% chance of being picked by at least one other agent; in nearly a quarter of cases, all four agents picked the same top product. In other words, whether you make the default list largely determines whether a product gets seen.

And that list is short. Muse is the only one of the four that fully exposes its research logs, and they show it almost always starts with its own Meta catalog and pulls at most 50 candidates. When it also searches via browser—not every time—it looks at only three product pages on average. The high overlap among other agents suggests their search sets are similarly small.

fig.title: Muse's candidate pool: up to 50 options and just 3 pages on average
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: blue is the default starting point (Meta catalog), amber is closer review and final selection
fig.note: Based on Muse's public research logs; the 1 final recommendation is illustrative

blocks.p: How do you get onto that shortlist? Lean into spike use cases: prove you're stronger for more specific people or scenarios. The hairdryer test is the clearest example—agents were asked to choose between the Shark FlexStyle and Dyson Airwrap. In a broad comparison, the cheaper Shark won 91% of the time. But as soon as the user said 'fine or color-treated hair,' Dyson won 51%; when they said 'daily use,' Dyson's win rate jumped to 88%. Specific needs force agents to weigh features like weight, maximum temperature, and noise, making Dyson's premium easier to justify.

fig.title: Specific needs flip the default recommendation
fig.subtitle: Amber marks scenarios where a specific condition flips the pick; values are the share of runs won by that product
fig.note: Shark's 91% means the cheaper Shark was selected; the other two figures are Dyson's win rates

blocks.p: Software follows the same logic. Asked broadly for 'graphic design software,' agents nominated Canva 78% of the time and Adobe never made the list. But when a user mentioned 'team templates,' Adobe appeared frequently; when they said they needed 'professional-level output,' Adobe was picked every time. So don't fight the default answer on broad requests—win the requests with a specific context.

sections.h: Agents aren't normal search: memory first, then your product page

blocks.p: Traditional LLMs find products through training data and web search, and tend to surface a few good options from review sites, news, and forums—not necessarily products you can buy. Agents are different: they check user memory first (stored preferences), then their own connectors and catalogs, and only then do external research. Muse and Dots use proprietary search systems; Grok Bot and Instinct use Exa.

fig.title: Agents check memory and their own catalogs before searching the web
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: blue is the central 'agent' actor, amber is what agents do that traditional models don't

blocks.p: Key difference: agents are more likely than traditional LLMs to visit direct or third-party product pages. So whether an agent can read your website determines whether it can figure out what your product does, what it costs, and what limits apply—and whether you make the final list.

Software works the same way. The authors asked Dots to generate 10 ads from a product photo and let the agent pick its own image-generation tool. It checked Midjourney first, found the official guidance says there is no general API and automated use is almost always prohibited, and gave up. It then went to Ideogram, where it traced a path from the product page to an API and an official MCP (a protocol for connecting software tools) integration—the docs even include code to generate and download an image—and easily made the choice. Giving agents a clear path beats a polished landing page built for humans.

sections.h: Agents do the math: returns, discounts, and trust all factor in

blocks.p: Agents are ruthless optimizers: they calculate the fully loaded cost of a product, including shipping, subscription lengths, return or refund policies, and even warranties. The starkest number: at the same price, agents chose the retailer with the better return policy 86% of the time (free returns, longer return window, refund to the original payment method).

Quince is the poster child: it ranks in the top 15 retailers by observed agent spend, yet it isn't a top 15 global retailer. Its page for a $50 cashmere sweater puts price, free shipping, inventory, and reviews near the top, and compares directly against traditional retail prices. Software is similar: domain registration tool Porkbun ranks #9 by observed agent transactions and #1 in the technology category, beating Cloudflare (#17) and GoDaddy (#112)—even though the latter two register 2.6x and 4.8x as many domains per month. Muse and Dots both favor its transparent pricing and lack of the discounted first-year price that jumps later.

But price has a breaking point. In one run, Grok Bot passed over a $200 Sonos speaker for a $250 option from an authorized dealer, citing warranty coverage. Across 275 real-store comparisons, agents chose the more expensive but more trusted seller 72% of the time. On discounts: under 10% did nothing; 10%–50% helped, but agents still picked the cheaper, less trusted option only 24% of the time; once a discount exceeded 50%, agents steered clear—if it looked too good to be true, they dismissed it.

sections.h: Each agent has its own taste: channels, evidence, and presentation vary

blocks.p: The four agents behave like four different people. Some differences come from bot-blocking: in Amazon checkout tests, Grok Bot reached the cart every time, while Muse, Instinct, and Dots got stuck every time. Channel preferences are strong too: Grok Bot linked to Amazon in 17.5% of runs, while no other agent topped 1.6%; Muse linked to Walmart in 26% of answers and Best Buy in 22%.

They also trust different evidence. Muse rarely cites reviews, mentioning them in just 10% of its recommendations versus 30%–41% for the others; Dots cites professional product tests in 11.4% of runs, while no other agent tops 3.7%; Instinct doesn't take ratings at face value—in 26 tiebreaker tests, 'better reviews' won only 4 times, while returns and cancellation terms mattered more to it.

fig.title: Four agents, four sets of tastes and channels
fig.subtitle: All values are shares observed in testing
fig.note: Dots also cites professional product tests in 11.4% of runs; Instinct won only 4 of 26 tiebreakers on 'better reviews'; Grok Bot reached the cart in every Amazon checkout test (not completed payment); the source gives only an aggregate 30%–41% range for the three agents other than Muse.

blocks.p: Presentation differs too. Asked for an AI notes tool for in-person meetings, Grok Bot and Instinct both ended up recommending Granola, with similar reasons (works on existing devices, privacy, convenience), but Instinct created a polished presentation page while Grok Bot gave a straight answer and even offered to take the notes itself first. So the same product can be 'sold' very differently depending on the agent.

sections.h: Go where agents already are: marketplaces, aggregators, and checkout

blocks.p: Agents like to begin and end searches on aggregators and marketplaces, where candidates are dense and easy to compare in one pass. Among the top 50 merchants by agent spend, nearly one-third of observed spend went to marketplaces and aggregators; add retailers that operate third-party marketplaces and the share rises to 46%; add conventional multi-brand retailers and it reaches 55%.

fig.title: Nearly one-third of top 50 merchant agent spend goes to marketplaces and aggregators
fig.subtitle: Amber is the narrowest, most direct measure; the next two add categories cumulatively
fig.note: The source says 'nearly one-third'; the chart uses 33% as an illustrative conversion

blocks.p: That share is clearly lifted by travel—the largest category of observed agent spend so far. In YipitData's sample, Expedia and Booking.com were the top two merchants by spend, with American Airlines #4 and United #6. In one live example, Hotel Zelos's refundable king room for December 4–6, 2026, cost $476.20 direct and $476 on Expedia, which also gave the agent a choice to pay now or at the property plus a PayPal option. (That example was a browser walkthrough; no reservation was submitted.) Unless the user explicitly asks to book direct, the agent's preference is clear.

For now, agents mostly rely on their own product catalogs and browser use to choose; external connectors are still rare. In tests from October 22 to November 8, Grok Bot offered to connect an app in only 5% of prompts, while the other three each did so in under 1%. But that's changing quickly: OpenAI's Businesses in ChatGPT lets merchants update their details and add product feeds with pricing and inventory; Meta connects its existing product catalog into Muse's search starting point; Shopify Catalog lets products be bought directly with Shop Pay.

Checkout is the final hurdle. On stores offering guest checkout, agents reached the last step of the checkout form 81% of the time; on stores requiring a logged-in account, every run stalled early—sometimes to ask the user for credentials, sometimes to switch merchants. For payments, Muse, Grok Bot, and Instinct all use Stripe's Link wallet. Muse can check out instantly at more than a million merchants that accept Link and issues a single-use virtual card elsewhere, with the user approving purchases in chat without giving the agent their real card number. After testing ended, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet for Dots on November 13, starting with U.S. Pro users.

sections.h: Method limitations and disclosures: what the original doesn't spell out

blocks.p: If you're treating this as empirical research, several methodological limits and boundaries need to be understood:

list: Sub-experiment sample sizes and extrapolation limits: the methodology notes that 'samples vary by experiment,' but the body does not disclose the specific denominator or full prompt set for each comparison. The tests cover only four specific personal agents from October 22 to November 8 and cannot be treated as equivalent to real users' natural shopping behavior or projected onto the whole consumer market.

YipitData panel limits: the spending panel runs through November 11, 2026; its tracking does not distinguish Muse from Instinct and excludes Amazon (even though 17.5% of Grok Bot's runs linked to Amazon in testing). Merchant rankings and dollar amounts refer only to that sample, not total merchant revenue, and travel accounts for the largest share.

Demo flows and timing changes: the Amazon checkout test only recorded whether agents reached the cart, and the Hotel Zelos example was a browser walkthrough with no reservation submitted. After testing, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet for Dots on November 13 for U.S. Pro users, and external connectors and retailer partnerships are changing quickly.

Identity of the four agents and Top 50 details: the original only clearly states that Muse connects to Meta's product catalog and Dots connects to ChatGPT Wallet; the full ownership and configuration of the other agents are not spelled out. The body also does not list all Top 50 merchants with their individual amounts.

Researcher and test partner disclosures: the article was written by partners at venture firm a16z, and the endnotes state that its funds' portfolio may include companies mentioned in the piece (investment list at a16z.com/investment-list/; disclosures at a16z.com/disclosures). Partner The Prompting Company itself sells AI agent discovery and purchase optimization services to businesses, and the authors close by soliciting startups in the same space.

blocks.p: The value: if you sell anything—physical products, SaaS, domains, hotels—these tests are the first to quantify how agents choose, and can directly guide product pages, pricing, and channels.

The cost: acting on these findings means maintaining an agent-readable website, publishing transparent pricing and return policies, getting products into aggregators and marketplaces, supporting guest checkout, and dealing with each agent's different tastes.

list: If you're a brand or e-commerce seller: test how your site looks to an agent, and put price, shipping, inventory, reviews, and return policies near the top of the page.
If you build software or SaaS: give agents an API or MCP path—don't make them hit a wall the way Midjourney does.
If you run channel operations: don't focus only on people—claim space in the marketplaces and aggregators where agents already gather.
If you're just curious: the most counterintuitive finding is that your return policy is now marketing copy—it decided 86% of same-price, two-option choices.
